passages.t: ‘Come, bless the LORD’: the last Song of Ascents
passages.happening:
Psalm 134 is the last of the Songs of Ascents, and one of the shortest psalms. “A song of ascents. Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!” (verse 1). “Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!” (verse 2).

Then a blessing comes back. “May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The temple was never empty. Priests and Levites served in turns, and the musicians among the Levites “were on duty day and night” (1 Chronicles 9:33). Lamps were tended and gates were guarded through the dark hours. Verse 1 speaks to those night workers. To ‘serve’ here is literally to stand: a servant stood before his master, ready.

Lifting the hands was the ordinary way to pray and praise in Israel. People raised open palms toward the sanctuary.

The psalm has two voices. In verses 1 and 2 someone, perhaps pilgrims leaving or arriving, calls on the night servants to bless the LORD. In verse 3 a blessing comes back. It echoes the blessing God gave the priests to speak over Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24).

So the fifteen Songs of Ascents, which began in Psalm 120 far away among people who hate peace, end in the house of the LORD at night, with blessing going up and blessing coming down. ‘The Maker of heaven and earth’, named in Psalms 121 and 124, is named again here at the end.
passages.later: Paul wrote, “I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension” (1 Timothy 2:8). John saw a great crowd before God's throne who “serve Him day and night in His temple” (Revelation 7:15).
passages.asks:
Some service to God is done at night, unseen: a parent awake with a sick child, a nurse on a late shift, a person praying alone when they cannot sleep. Psalm 134 says that God sees night work, and that it can be worship.

And it gives you a blessing to take home: ‘May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you.’ You may also speak it over someone else.
